articles.title: Freeze, fraud alert or monitoring? What to do after a breach
articles.excerpt: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring each protect different parts of your financial life after a data breach…
articles.fullText:
A data breach notice can leave you with plenty of questions. Should you freeze your credit? Is a fraud alert enough? Do you need an identity monitoring service ? The right response depends on what information was exposed and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's the important distinction. A company saying your information was involved in a breach does not automatically mean someone has opened an account in your name.
An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves attention, but it does not always prove fraud occurred. However, once you confirm someone has used your information fraudulently, the situation becomes more urgent. So, which protection should you choose? Let's look at what each one actually does.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
YOU HAVE A CREDIT FREEZE; IT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH
A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file. It makes it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because most lenders need to review your credit information before approving an application. Credit freezes are completely free. You must place one separately with each of the three major credit bureaus:
A freeze stays in place until you remove it, and it does not affect your credit score. If you apply for a mortgage, car loan or credit card, you may need to temporarily lift the freeze so the lender can review your report. You can do that for free.
Employment and tenant-screening checks follow different rules and generally are not blocked by a credit freeze. A freeze is a strong option if your Social Security number was exposed or you simply want to reduce the risk of someone opening new credit in your name. However, it cannot protect an existing bank account, stop a scam payment or remove a fraudulent account that was already opened.
A fraud alert tells lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity before approving new credit. Unlike a freeze, a fraud alert does not restrict access to your credit report. Instead, it warns lenders that someone may be trying to use your information.
There are two main types:
A fraud alert can be convenient if you're actively applying for a mortgage, loan or credit card and don't want to manage multiple credit freezes . Still, it offers less control than a freeze because lenders can continue accessing your credit file after completing the required identity checks. If someone has already opened an account fraudulently, placing an alert can help reduce additional risk. However, you'll still need to contact the creditor and dispute the fraudulent account.
Identity monitoring watches for certain changes involving your personal or financial information and notifies you when suspicious activity appears.
Depending on the service, those alerts may include:
Monitoring is useful because it can give you an earlier warning that someone may be misusing your information. But there's an important limitation. Monitoring generally alerts you after suspicious activity is detected. It does not necessarily prevent that activity from happening. And no service can monitor everything. For example, basic credit monitoring may not detect an email account takeover, medical identity theft or a payment you authorized after being tricked by a scammer.
The right protection depends on what happened to your information and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's what to do in each situation.
Start by reviewing the breach notice to understand exactly what information was involved. If passwords were exposed, change them immediately. Use unique passwords for each account and enable multifactor authentication, especially on your primary email account. If your Social Security number was compromised, consider freezing your credit with all three major bureaus right away. You can also take advantage of free credit monitoring offered by the affected company, if available. Just verify the offer through the company's official website.
An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves a closer look, but it doesn't always mean someone has stolen your identity. Contact the company listed on the inquiry using its official website or customer service number. Ask whether an application was submitted using your information. You should also review your credit reports from all three bureaus. You can get free weekly credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If you suspect someone is trying to open credit in your name, consider placing a free credit freeze immediately while you investigate. You can also add a fraud alert.
If you confirm that someone opened an account fraudulently, act immediately.
Keep copies of your reports, correspondence and case numbers while the investigation continues.
A credit freeze alone won't help if someone already has access to one of your existing accounts. Contact the financial institution or service provider immediately. If your bank account is involved, report unauthorized transactions and ask what protections can be placed on the account. If your email was compromised, change the password from a trusted device, review recovery information and sign out of unfamiliar sessions. And if your phone suddenly loses service for no obvious reason, contact your wireless carrier immediately. An unexpected loss of service can be a warning sign of a SIM-swap attack.
WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS
You don't need to spend the entire week worrying about what might happen. However, you should address the most serious risks right away.
Also, watch out for follow-up scams. Criminals sometimes use major data breaches as an excuse to contact people with fake monitoring offers or recovery services. They may ask for your Social Security number, passwords or payment information. Don't trust a caller simply because they know details about the breach. Instead, verify offers by going directly to the affected company's official website.
Here's the easiest way to think about these protections.
You can use more than one tool. In fact, a credit freeze and monitoring service can complement each other. Just remember that none of these options replaces contacting your bank, creditor or service provider when fraud has already occurred.
A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name, but it won't alert you to every suspicious change involving your personal information. An identity monitoring service can complement that protection by watching for certain warning signs.
Depending on the plan, you may also have access to identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate disputes, documentation and recovery after identity theft. Neither tool guarantees complete protection, but together they can help you prevent certain problems and respond more quickly when suspicious activity appears.
Not all monitoring services offer the same protections. Before choosing one, consider these features:
Keep in mind that identity monitoring cannot prevent every form of fraud or guarantee that suspicious activity will always be detected. You'll still need to contact your bank, credit card company or other affected institution directly if you discover unauthorized activity.
The bottom line: A credit freeze can help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts, while identity monitoring can help you spot certain warning signs sooner. Using both can give you broader protection and make it easier to respond when something goes wrong.
Ask one question first: am I trying to block new credit, receive an early warning or recover from confirmed fraud? A freeze focuses on blocking access, a fraud alert adds verification and monitoring provides visibility. You may use more than one, but you do not need to activate every tool simply because a breach occurred.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE
One thing I've noticed about data breaches is that most people don't realize how vulnerable their personal information can be until something goes wrong. And by then, the damage may already be done. That's why I think it's smart to be proactive. A free credit freeze is a great place to start, but it only protects one part of your financial life.
What I like about an identity protection service is that it adds another layer of protection by monitoring for suspicious activity that you might otherwise miss. And if someone does steal your identity, having access to restoration specialists can make a stressful situation easier to manage. No service can stop every scam, but having someone watching for warning signs and helping you respond can make a real difference. For me, it's about getting ahead of the problem rather than finding out about it after the damage is done.

No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW
Finding child sexual abuse material online has become more complicated as AI-generated content spreads. Many existing detection systems use digital fingerprints , called hashes, to recognize previously identified abusive files. However, newly created material may have no matching fingerprint. OpenAI's new classifier examines visual signs of potential child sexual abuse material, also known as CSAM. That allows it to flag suspected abuse even when the content has never been identified before.
The system assigns scores to potentially abusive pictures so human reviewers can decide which cases need attention first. OpenAI says it developed and evaluated the technology with help from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) at missingkids.org/ . The company is offering the classifier at no cost to vetted organizations through its API. That could give smaller child protection teams access to detection technology they otherwise couldn't afford.
OpenAI says its early testing produced encouraging results. In an evaluation involving pictures uploaded to its systems, the company compared the new classifier with its existing protections. The findings suggest the new tool could flag 48% fewer pictures for review while detecting roughly the same amount of abusive material. Pictures flagged by the new classifier were also about twice as likely to contain abuse.
Outside organizations reported additional results. AI platform Fal said its reviewers confirmed 72% of high-confidence flags as previously unidentified CSAM. Meanwhile, SafetyKit reported that the classifier detected 90% of cases involving drawings or animations that sexualize children in its evaluation. These results come from OpenAI and participating organizations. Independent testing will help determine how reliably the technology performs across different platforms.
INSTAGRAM'S AI MAY CATCH TEENS LYING ABOUT THEIR AGE
OpenAI is also changing how ChatGPT responds when someone attempts to find child sexual abuse material. New warnings will interrupt those attempts and explain the harm caused by sexualizing children. The warnings specifically address AI-generated material, which can cause serious harm even when a picture has been digitally fabricated. Along with displaying a warning, OpenAI says it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. The warning will also direct the person toward specialist support designed to help prevent harmful behavior.
Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions or permanent account closure. OpenAI says they could also result in reports to authorities. The new warnings focus on attempts to find abusive material. Under its existing policies, OpenAI says it bans accounts and reports attempts to generate or upload CSAM to NCMEC. The company developed the warnings with input from child protection organizations and researchers who study ways to interrupt harmful online behavior. However, whether these interventions prevent future abuse will require continued evaluation.
OpenAI is expanding its work with organizations investigating online child exploitation. The company says it has begun participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program, which allows organizations to share information about suspected exploitation across platforms. It's also introducing specialized AI tools and training for child safety law enforcement units. The first investigative tool will help authorized teams review lengthy chat logs and records obtained through legal processes. Investigators can use it to identify potential connections and organize timelines, with findings linked to source material. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. OpenAI is also publishing guidance to help developers detect suspected abuse and establish procedures for reviewing potentially harmful content.
IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?
You can't control every way someone might misuse a child's photo . However, a few steps can help families reduce exposure and respond if something happens.
Most importantly, make sure children know they can come to you without automatically losing access to their devices. That conversation may help them speak up before harmful content spreads further.
HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM
If you're a parent or grandparent, these developments could help improve protection against AI-generated child sexual abuse material. However, the new classifier works behind the scenes. Its impact will depend on how widely organizations adopt it and how effectively their safety teams respond to warnings.
The scale of the problem is alarming. According to NCMEC, its CyberTipline received more than 400,000 reports involving generative AI in 2025. These reports cover several categories of AI-related child exploitation, although not all involved the creation or sharing of AI-generated abuse material.
I'm glad to see OpenAI making this detection technology available to vetted organizations for free. The early results are encouraging, especially if investigators can spend less time reviewing false alarms and more time identifying children who need help. I also support putting consequences behind ChatGPT's warnings. A 24-hour suspension sends a stronger message than simply telling someone their request violates the rules. We've already seen how AI-generated content can be used to harm children, and technology companies need to stay ahead of those who misuse their tools. OpenAI is taking steps in the right direction, and I hope other AI companies follow its lead.

The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate decreased from 3.9% in the three months from July to September to 3.8% in the period from August to October, the Census & Statistics Department announced today.

The underemployment rate remained at 2%.

Total employment was 3,653,800, down 1,200 from the previous three-month period, while the labour force dropped by around 5,800 to 3,804,200.

“The Government will continue to closely monitor the evolving external uncertainties for their potential implications on corporate hiring sentiments and provide job-seekers with appropriate support," Mr Sun said.

articles.title: AI mosquito trap targets deadly dengue outbreak
articles.excerpt: USF researchers built an AI mosquito trap with over 98% accuracy as Florida battles its largest dengue outbreak in decades…
articles.fullText:
You probably aren't thinking much about mosquitoes in November. In much of the country, cooler weather has sent those annoying little bloodsuckers into hiding. But in Florida, mosquitoes are still causing serious trouble. The state is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades, and hundreds of people have caught the virus without leaving the state.
Now, researchers at the University of South Florida have developed an AI mosquito trap that could help health officials find dangerous mosquito species much faster. It can identify mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. And with dengue still spreading in Florida, the timing couldn't be more important.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE
If you thought mosquito season ended when summer did, Florida has a different story to tell. According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County has recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, the county's largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, health officials have reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. That means people contracted the virus from mosquitoes in the area rather than while traveling overseas.
The Tampa area has been hit especially hard. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak . Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain. In serious cases, it can lead to life-threatening complications. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.
On November 13, Hillsborough County announced that it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments to help contain the outbreak. County officials say mosquito surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area.
And here's why we're talking about this in November. While mosquitoes have largely disappeared from colder parts of the country, they can remain active in warmer states. Florida's outbreak shows that the threat doesn't disappear simply because summer is over. Meanwhile, a new generation of technology could give communities a better way to respond before mosquito populations get out of control.
The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by researchers at the University of South Florida. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have been developing the system through research dating back to 2018. Their goal is to help mosquito control teams identify the insects they're catching without spending days examining them under a microscope.
The trap itself looks fairly straightforward. Workers can hang it from a low tree branch or place it on the ground. A light or bait attracts mosquitoes, and a small fan pulls them inside. Once the insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. Artificial intelligence then compares those images against a large database to determine which mosquito species have been captured.
But the technology goes further. It can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. That's useful information because female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. The researchers say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing.
GOOGLE WANTS TO RELEASE MILLIONS OF MOSQUITOES
Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. That's valuable work, but when health officials are trying to track a disease outbreak, waiting several days can slow their response. Digitomy wants to shorten that process dramatically. Its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured mosquito species the same day. That could help mosquito control teams see where potentially dangerous species are appearing and decide where to concentrate their efforts.
This is especially important with Aedes aegypti , the mosquito species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases. Knowing which ones are present can help officials make better decisions. There's one important point to understand. The trap identifies mosquito species capable of carrying disease. It does not automatically prove that a captured mosquito is infected with dengue. Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus.
What I find particularly interesting is what happens after the trap identifies a mosquito. Digitomy can send that information to a mapping dashboard, allowing mosquito control teams to see where certain species are appearing. The goal is to give mosquito control teams access to that information the same day, helping them identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. Think about how useful that could be during an outbreak. If several traps begin detecting more Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in one neighborhood, officials could investigate that area and consider targeted mosquito control measures. Instead of waiting for more people to become sick, they could use surveillance data to guide their response.
The researchers have already integrated trap information into a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard at mosquitodashboard.org/. That system also incorporates more than half a million citizen science reports. The idea is to combine information from automated traps with observations from people who help track mosquitoes. Digitomy's technology could also complement an existing early warning system developed by Carney for dengue and West Nile virus . Together, these tools could give public health departments a clearer view of mosquito activity across communities. Of course, detecting mosquitoes early doesn't guarantee that an outbreak can be prevented. But faster information could help officials respond sooner, particularly in areas where mosquito control resources are limited.
Digitomy has already tested its technology at the University of South Florida and worked with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. The researchers are also preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County, where Florida's dengue outbreak has been especially severe. The startup is working with USF's Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito trap manufacturers. That could allow companies to add the technology to equipment they already produce.
Digitomy is working toward commercial availability by licensing its AI technology to established mosquito trap manufacturers. For now, the university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. The company also received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation's Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026. The funding is intended to help accelerate the licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online education platform that would allow mosquito control professionals and the public to practice identifying mosquito species using images and AI-generated feedback.
THIRD PERSON DIES AFTER MOSQUITO IS REPORTEDLY TRAPPED ON PLANE TO GERMANY IN 'AIRPORT MALARIA' PHENOMENON
You probably won't be hanging a Digitomy trap in your backyard anytime soon. But that doesn't mean this technology couldn't eventually affect your community. If mosquito control departments adopt smarter surveillance systems, they may be able to identify dangerous mosquito populations sooner and make better decisions about where to intervene. And even though we're heading into November, people living in warmer areas still need to pay attention to mosquito activity. If you're traveling to Florida or another place where mosquitoes remain active, taking precautions is important.
For now, the best protection is still fairly simple. Empty standing water from flowerpots and other outdoor containers because mosquitoes can breed in surprisingly small amounts of water. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent when spending time outdoors. Wearing long sleeves and pants can also help reduce exposed skin. We've covered some useful products that can help keep mosquitoes away, including repellents and outdoor gadgets.
You can find them in our guide to mosquito and tick repellents at CyberGuy.com
I think this is one of those uses of AI that could make a real difference in people's lives. Most of us see mosquitoes as an annoying part of summer. But Florida's dengue outbreak is a reminder that these tiny insects can cause serious health problems, even late in the year. What interests me about Digitomy is the possibility of giving mosquito control teams information while they still have time to act. The technology looks promising, especially with its reported accuracy in laboratory testing. But I want to see how it performs in real-world conditions before calling it a breakthrough. If it works as researchers hope, communities could have a valuable new tool to help protect people from mosquito-borne diseases. And that's a use of AI I can get behind.
Would you feel safer knowing AI-powered mosquito traps were monitoring your neighborhood? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

Candidates planning to enrol in the Scheme for Admission of Hong Kong Students to Mainland Higher Education Institutions can apply online from December 1 to 31, the Education Bureau said today.

The number of Chinese Mainland institutions participating in the scheme will increase to 169 for the 2027/28 academic year. Located in 21 provinces or municipalities and two autonomous regions, they will accept applications from candidates taking the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) Examination in 2027.

The Education Bureau encourages Hong Kong students to study on the Chinese Mainland via the scheme, thereby seizing opportunities to learn about the country’s social, economic and cultural landscape, and to bolster their own development.

The bureau said it will continue discussions to enable more renowned Mainland institutions to participate in the scheme, with a view to providing students with multiple higher education pathways and opportunities to connect with the country’s development.

Students should review their submitted application details online before January 10, 2027, while those providing supplementary information should do so before January 23. Students who pass the application verification process should pay the enrolment fee by January 31.

Institutions will announce admission results in late July next year. They may also arrange for supplementary enrolment depending on the enrolment situation.

articles.title: Fake AI event invites target Microsoft and Google logins
articles.excerpt: Fake OpenAI event pages promise free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions, then trick employees into handing over Microsoft and Google account credentials.
articles.fullText:
An invitation to an exclusive OpenAI event lands in your inbox. It promises a look at the latest AI tools and even offers three months of ChatGPT Pro for free. All you have to do is register using your work account. Sounds like a pretty good deal, right? Well, before you click that registration button, there's something you should know. Cybercriminals are using fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving them access to their Microsoft and Google accounts. And some of these attacks can get past the extra security checks many of us rely on.
According to a new report from Push Security, attackers have created convincing event registration pages impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The concerning part is how easily an invitation that appears legitimate can lead to someone handing over access to their work account. Here's what researchers discovered and how to protect yourself.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
The attackers are taking advantage of the growing interest in artificial intelligence . After all, plenty of employees want to learn how AI can make their jobs easier. A free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention. The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promote events that appear to come from recognizable technology companies. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams." The registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. Another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12. Visitors could supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share."
Researchers also identified a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026. That page was no longer active when they investigated it. These pages impersonated legitimate technology companies, and the advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme. Push Security did not suggest that OpenAI, SpaceX or Anthropic operated these fraudulent events. And here's where things get especially concerning. The fake websites tell visitors they must sign in using their corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. That request opens the door to the phishing attack.
The criminals have put considerable effort into making these invitations appear credible. Rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website, they use familiar online services to help disguise where the links lead. Push Security found that the campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier. Earlier related attacks also used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. As a result, someone checking an invitation might see a familiar service before reaching the malicious registration page. Researchers have not confirmed the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign.
Once someone reaches the suspicious site, another familiar feature appears. A Cloudflare security challenge asks visitors to confirm they are human. You have probably encountered similar checks while shopping or visiting legitimate websites. However, criminals can use them too. In this campaign, the challenge also made it harder for automated security scanners to examine the malicious pages. After completing the check, visitors arrive at what looks like a professional event registration website. They're presented with two familiar buttons: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google." Depending on which button someone selects, the attackers launch a different method designed to capture access to that account.
This is where the attack gets clever. If someone selects "Continue with Microsoft," the phishing website connects to a service called Kali365. It's a phishing-as-a-service platform that criminals can use to carry out account attacks. Kali365 generates a Microsoft device authentication code. The fake registration page then instructs the visitor to copy that code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in website.
Now, here's why that can fool someone. Microsoft's device authentication process is real. You may have used something similar when connecting a streaming device to an account. However, the attacker started this authentication request. When the victim enters the supplied code and approves the sign-in, Microsoft can issue authentication tokens to the attacker's session.
Those tokens may provide access to Microsoft 365 resources without the attacker needing the account password. And the attack may continue from there. Push Security found that the campaign redirects Microsoft users to another phishing service called VoidProxy after the device code step. That second stage attempts to capture their password and authenticated session cookie. A successful compromise could expose company email or documents stored in Microsoft 365. Other connected workplace applications may also be at risk, depending on the permissions and access associated with the compromised account.
The Google option takes another approach. When visitors click "Continue with Google," the phishing page opens a pop-up that appears to contain Google's familiar sign-in screen. However, that login process runs through VoidProxy, which acts as an intermediary between the person signing in and Google's actual authentication service.
As someone enters their credentials, the phishing service can capture the information. It can also intercept certain multifactor authentication responses and steal session cookies. So, what exactly is a session cookie? Think of it as a digital pass that helps a website remember you've already signed in. Once your identity has been verified, that cookie can allow you to continue using your account without entering your password on every page.
If a criminal obtains a usable session cookie, they may be able to reuse that authenticated session and gain access without completing the usual login process again. That's why these attacks are particularly dangerous for people who believe that enabling multifactor authentication automatically protects them from every account takeover attempt. It's important to note that Push Security documented the malicious infrastructure and blocked visits to the phishing pages. Its report did not establish how many accounts, if any, were successfully compromised through this campaign.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
The attackers are combining two phishing services behind the same registration pages. Kali365 targets Microsoft's device authentication process, while VoidProxy targets authenticated login sessions. Meanwhile, the fake event websites borrow the appearance of familiar brands. The criminals can also change their websites and event themes as older pages get discovered. Researchers also discovered that the fraudulent registration pages could automatically display content in a visitor's language. That allowed the attackers to adapt the same phishing campaign for people in different regions without creating entirely new websites. Push Security identified two phishing kits used to create the fake event pages. The researchers call them ZoomMock and MSDRoot. They found evidence suggesting the same operators were responsible for both kits, although the connection was not conclusively established.
Researchers also found no evidence linking the developers of Kali365 and VoidProxy. Instead, they believe the attackers behind the event campaign are customers of both phishing services. The result is an attack that can appear credible at several points. A shortened link may use a recognized service. A security challenge can look legitimate. Even the Microsoft authentication page can be genuine. For employees who regularly attend virtual meetings or participate in industry webinars, that familiarity could make the scam harder to recognize.
In response to our request for comment, a Microsoft spokesperson said, "We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect our customers from evolving threats. Microsoft Defender includes detections to block the threats identified in the report."
We also reached out to Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX for comment but did not receive responses before our deadline.
A few careful habits can significantly reduce your chances of falling for these attacks. Here's how to protect yourself.
If you receive an unexpected invitation from OpenAI, SpaceX or another technology company, take a moment to check whether the event actually exists. Open a new browser tab and visit the organization's official website yourself. Look for the event through its verified channels. If necessary, contact the organizer using information obtained independently of the invitation. Be especially careful when an unfamiliar event requests your corporate account credentials.
An invitation promising premium AI access may sound appealing, especially when the offer appears to come from a respected technology company. However, the promise of something valuable can encourage people to act before checking the details. If registration requires you to sign in with a work account to receive a reward, verify the offer independently before proceeding.
This is one of the most important lessons from the campaign. If a website asks you to copy a device authentication code and enter it on a Microsoft page, consider whether you initiated a legitimate device sign-in. If you were simply registering for a webinar, that unexpected device code request should raise concerns. Even a legitimate Microsoft authentication webpage can become part of a phishing attack when criminals trick you into approving their request. Pay attention to any Microsoft sign-in prompt asking you to approve access. Even if the website address is legitimate, you could be authorizing a session started by a criminal.
THE BEST DEFENSE AGAINST HIGH-TECH AI SCAMS IS LOW-TECH SKEPTICISM, EXPERT WARNS
Before entering account credentials, examine the website address and consider how you arrived there. A page displaying familiar branding may still belong to a criminal. Shortened links can also conceal the final destination. Whenever possible, open Microsoft or Google directly through a trusted bookmark or the official website. Remember that a padlock icon and HTTPS connection do not guarantee that a website is trustworthy.
Continue using multifactor authentication , even though some phishing attacks can defeat certain forms of it. For stronger protection, consider phishing-resistant authentication, such as FIDO2 security keys or supported passkeys. These methods can help prevent attackers from stealing credentials through fraudulent login websites. While these methods offer stronger protection against phishing, they cannot guarantee protection if an attacker obtains a valid authenticated session through another method. However, no single security measure stops every possible attack. Organizations should also consider additional controls to protect authenticated sessions and reduce the risk of stolen tokens being reused. Microsoft recommends restricting device code authentication wherever it isn't necessary. IT administrators can apply those restrictions through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies after reviewing legitimate business needs.
Strong antivirus software and browser protections can help identify suspicious links and dangerous websites before you interact with them. Look for protection that helps detect phishing pages and malicious downloads. Keep your browser and security tools updated so they can benefit from the latest available protections. However, remember that attackers frequently create new websites to evade detection. Security software can reduce your exposure, but it cannot guarantee that every fraudulent invitation will be blocked. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com
If you've already clicked on a suspicious event invitation, don't panic. What you do next depends on how far you got in the sign-in process. Here are the steps to take to protect your accounts.
The sooner you report suspicious activity, the better the chances of stopping unauthorized access before more damage occurs.
Criminals know people are eager to keep up with AI, and they're using that interest to make their scams more convincing. An invitation offering free ChatGPT Pro or access to an exclusive event sounds pretty tempting. But what really concerns me is that you can land on Microsoft's actual sign-in page and still give a hacker access to your account. Think about that. Even checking the website address may not be enough to protect you. So before you sign up for that next AI event, take a minute to make sure it's legitimate. I'd rather miss out on a free offer than hand a criminal access to my work account.
Have you ever received an invitation to an online event that seemed too good to be true? What made you suspicious? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
